distance-and-margin-based-models.text: Some classifiers never fit a coefficient per feature. Instead they reason about geometry: which training points sit near this one, how wide a gap separates the two classes, how far a point falls on the correct side of a boundary. That geometric view splits into a few distinct ideas. One family predicts by looking at neighbours, which makes the definition of near the whole ballgame. Another family draws a boundary and asks how much clearance it has, then finds a way to bend that boundary without ever computing the bent coordinates. And one works on probabilities rather than geometry, but shares the family trait of skipping gradient fitting entirely, which makes it brutally fast and surprisingly hard to beat on text.
distance-and-margin-based-models.deep_text:
Five units sit under this heading, and they make the most sense read in that order. K-Nearest Neighbours comes first because it is the purest expression of the geometric idea: store the training set, and at prediction time let the closest examples vote. It has no training step worth the name, which makes it the cleanest place to see what distance-based reasoning actually buys you and what it costs.

Distance Metrics and Scaling Sensitivity follows immediately, because the neighbours unit leaves one question dangling. Nearest according to what? The answer is not a detail. Choosing a metric and putting features on comparable footing is what decides whether a distance-based model works at all, and the same question resurfaces later in clustering and in similarity search, so it deserves a unit of its own rather than a footnote.

Support Vector Machines and the Maximum Margin then flips the perspective. Rather than consulting local neighbours, it commits to a single global boundary and picks the one with the largest buffer around it. That objective turns out to depend only on a handful of training points, which is a very different relationship to the data than storing all of it.

The Kernel Trick comes fourth because it is a modification to the margin machinery, not a standalone algorithm. It answers what to do when no straight boundary works, and it does so through a substitution that is easier to appreciate once you already know what the margin formulation looks like.

Naive Bayes and Conditional Independence closes the group, and it reasons about probability rather than geometry. It belongs here because it shares what unites the others: it classifies without iteratively fitting a weight per feature, reading its parameters straight off counts in a single pass over the data. That makes it the fastest baseline in this group and still a strong one on text, where the independence assumption it makes is wrong in principle and forgiving in practice. Read together, these five give you the main alternatives to fitting weights by gradient descent.

k-nearest-neighbours.text: K-Nearest Neighbours has no training phase. You keep the labelled examples, and when a new point arrives you find the k closest ones and let them vote — majority label for classification, average for regression. That is the entire algorithm. Everything interesting lives in the choices around it: how big k is, and how you measure closeness, which is a subject in its own right. Small k tracks the data tightly and picks up noise; large k smooths the boundary and eventually just predicts the majority class everywhere. Prediction is the expensive part, since every query scans the stored set.
k-nearest-neighbours.deep_text:
Picture a fraud classifier with 10,000 labelled transactions and two features, amount and seconds since the account's last transaction. A new charge comes in. With k=5, you compute the distance from that charge to all 10,000 stored points, sort, take the five nearest, and count labels. If four of them are fraud, you predict fraud, and the vote share of 0.8 doubles as a rough confidence score. Nothing was fitted, no parameters were learned; the training set is the model.

The choice of k is a bias-variance dial you can see directly. At k=1, every training point is classified correctly by definition, because its nearest neighbour is itself, and the decision boundary becomes a jagged mosaic that wraps around individual noisy points. At k=500 in a 10,000-point set, the prediction is close to the global class ratio and the boundary is nearly flat. Choose k by cross-validation, and note that odd values avoid ties in binary problems. Distances are computed in whatever coordinate system your features happen to live in, so the metric choice and feature scaling determine the neighbourhoods entirely — that question belongs to its own unit and it is not optional.

The misconception worth killing is that KNN is cheap because there is no training. The cost simply moves. Fitting is free; every single prediction is a scan of the entire stored dataset, which is O(n·d) per query. Ten thousand points is nothing, but ten million points with 300 features on a latency budget is a different story, and that is why approximate nearest-neighbour indexes like k-d trees, ball trees, and HNSW graphs exist. A k-d tree helps in low dimensions and degrades toward brute force as dimensionality rises.

The other trap is dimensionality. In high-dimensional space, the distance between a query and its nearest neighbour and the distance to its farthest neighbour converge, so nearest stops carrying information. KNN on raw 5,000-dimensional bag-of-words vectors is usually poor; KNN on 128-dimensional learned embeddings is often excellent, which is exactly why embedding search works.

Reach for KNN when you have a modest dataset, a genuinely irregular decision boundary, and no need for a fast interpretable rule; when you want a strong baseline in ten lines; or when your data already lives as embeddings. Avoid it for high-dimensional raw features, for very large training sets under tight latency, and when many features are irrelevant, since irrelevant dimensions add noise to every distance without adding signal.

interview.question: Why does KNN often perform badly as the number of features grows, even when you add more training data?
interview.answer: In high dimensions distances concentrate: the ratio between the nearest and farthest neighbour distances approaches one, so the nearest points are barely nearer than random points. The neighbourhood stops being local in any meaningful sense. Adding data does not fix this, because the volume you need to cover grows exponentially with dimension. The practical fix is dimensionality reduction or learned embeddings rather than more rows.

interview.question: When would you choose KNN over a tree ensemble in production?
interview.answer: Mainly when the data already lives as embeddings and you need similarity semantics anyway — recommendation, deduplication, near-duplicate detection — where the same vector index serves retrieval and classification. Also when the training set changes constantly, since adding an example is just an insert with no retraining. Otherwise a gradient-boosted tree usually wins on accuracy, latency, and robustness to irrelevant features.

interview.question: How would you pick k, and what goes wrong at each extreme?
interview.answer: Cross-validate over a range and pick the k that minimises held-out error, favouring odd values in binary classification to avoid ties. At k=1 training accuracy is perfect and meaningless — the model memorises noise and variance is maximal. At very large k the prediction collapses toward the majority class and you lose the local structure that motivated using KNN in the first place.

distance-metrics-and-scaling-sensitivity.text: Any model that compares points by distance inherits whatever units your features arrived in. If income runs from 20,000 to 200,000 and age runs from 20 to 80, the squared difference in income dominates every distance computation, and age contributes essentially nothing — you have silently built a model on income alone. Rescaling the columns first is what makes them comparable. Then the metric itself becomes a real choice: Euclidean distance measures straight-line separation, Manhattan sums coordinate-wise differences and is more forgiving of a single mismatched feature, and cosine similarity throws away vector length and compares direction only.
distance-metrics-and-scaling-sensitivity.deep_text:
Take two customers. A is 25 years old with income 50,000; B is 60 years old with income 51,000. The age gap is 35 years, a huge difference in any sensible sense, and the income gap is 1,000, which is noise. Euclidean distance on the raw values is the square root of 35 squared plus 1,000 squared, roughly 1,000.6. The 35-year gap moved the distance by about 0.6 out of 1,000. Now standardise: if age has standard deviation 15 and income has standard deviation 30,000, the scaled gaps become about 2.33 and 0.033, and age now dominates as it should. Nothing about the data changed — only the units — and the neighbourhoods flipped completely.

Which rescaling you use is a separate question, settled under feature engineering; what matters here is that until it is settled, the metric you pick is irrelevant, because every distance is really measuring one column. Once the columns are comparable, the choice of metric starts to carry the model. A useful sanity check is to compute a handful of nearest-neighbour lists before and after scaling: if the neighbours change wholesale, the raw units were doing the classifying, and any accuracy you measured beforehand was measuring the scale of your columns rather than the structure of your data.

The metrics differ in what they consider a big gap. Euclidean, the L2 norm, squares each coordinate difference, so one badly mismatched feature can dominate the total. Manhattan, L1, adds absolute differences, which spreads influence more evenly and tends to behave better in higher dimensions and with sparse data. Cosine similarity divides out both vectors' magnitudes and measures only the angle between them, which is why it is standard for text: a 200-word document and a 2,000-word document about the same topic point in nearly the same direction even though their raw counts are ten times apart. For binary or set-valued features, Jaccard or Hamming distance is a better fit than pretending the coordinates are continuous.

The misconception is that scaling is a tidiness step you can skip and recover later with hyperparameter tuning. It is not. No value of k, no kernel width, and no regularisation strength recovers a feature whose contribution to every distance is three orders of magnitude too small. The same applies to margin methods and to any regularised model, because a penalty on coefficients is also unit-dependent. Tree models are the genuine exception — they split on thresholds within a single feature, so monotone rescaling changes nothing.

One caution: scaling makes features comparable, not equally important. If you have 50 noise features and 3 useful ones, standardising gives the noise 50 dimensions' worth of vote. Feature selection or a learned metric, not scaling, is the remedy there.

interview.question: Which models require feature scaling and which are indifferent to it, and why?
interview.answer: Anything that computes distances or penalises coefficient magnitude needs it: KNN, k-means, SVMs, PCA, and any regularised linear model. Gradient descent on unscaled features also converges slowly because the loss surface becomes a stretched valley. Decision trees and their ensembles are indifferent, since a split compares a single feature against a threshold and any monotone rescaling produces the same ordering and the same split.

interview.question: Why is cosine similarity usually preferred over Euclidean distance for text?
interview.answer: Document vectors have length roughly proportional to document length, so Euclidean distance between a short and a long document on the same topic is large purely because of magnitude. Cosine normalises that away and compares only the direction, which is where the topical content lives. Note that on L2-normalised vectors the two are equivalent up to a monotone transform, so cosine is essentially Euclidean after normalisation.

interview.question: You fit a StandardScaler on the full dataset before splitting. What is the actual harm?
interview.answer: The mean and standard deviation used to transform the training data were computed partly from test rows, so information about the test distribution has leaked into training. Your held-out score becomes optimistically biased and stops being an estimate of production performance. The effect is small on large datasets and can be substantial on small ones or with heavy-tailed features; the fix is to fit inside the cross-validation pipeline.

support-vector-machines-and-the-maximum-.text: When two classes are separable, infinitely many lines separate them, and most of them sit uncomfortably close to some training point. A support vector machine picks the one line whose distance to the nearest point of either class is as large as possible. That gap is the margin, and the handful of points touching its edges are the support vectors — they alone determine the boundary, and moving any other training point does nothing. Real data overlaps, so a slack allowance lets some points sit inside or across the margin, with a cost parameter C setting how expensive each violation is.
support-vector-machines-and-the-maximum-.deep_text:
Consider a spam classifier with two features and 1,000 training emails. Many boundaries put every training email on the correct side, but a boundary that skims one metre past a legitimate email will misclassify the next slightly-different legitimate email. The maximum-margin boundary is the one placed as far as possible from both classes, which is the geometric expression of a preference for the least confident-looking fit. Formally the boundary is w·x + b = 0, the classes are pushed to satisfy y(w·x + b) at least 1, and the margin width is 2 divided by the norm of w. Maximising the margin therefore means minimising the norm of w subject to those constraints — a convex problem with a single global optimum, unlike a neural network's loss surface.

The striking consequence is sparsity in the training data. The solution can be written as a weighted sum over training points where nearly all weights are zero. Out of 1,000 emails, perhaps 40 have nonzero weight, and those 40 are the support vectors sitting on or inside the margin. Delete the other 960 and refit, and you get exactly the same boundary. This is a genuinely different relationship to data than a neighbour-based model, which needs all of it, or a linear regression, where every point tugs on the fit.

Perfect separation is rare, so the soft-margin formulation adds a slack variable per point measuring how far it violates its constraint, and penalises the total slack by C. Small C tolerates many violations and yields a wide, smooth margin that ignores individual awkward points — high bias, low variance. Large C insists on classifying training points correctly and produces a narrow margin that contorts around outliers, approaching the hard-margin case as C grows. C is the primary hyperparameter and there is no default that survives contact with a new dataset; cross-validate it on a log scale.

The common misconception is that maximising the margin is about training accuracy. It is not — many boundaries achieve identical training accuracy, and the margin is a tiebreaker among them chosen for its generalisation behaviour, since a wide margin means the boundary can be perturbed without changing predictions. A related confusion: the support vectors are not the points farthest from the boundary or the most typical examples. They are the borderline cases, the emails that are hardest to call.

SVMs are worth reaching for on small to medium datasets, especially wide ones where features outnumber samples, such as text classification and genomics, where the margin objective handles high dimensions gracefully. Skip them when n runs into the hundreds of thousands, since training scales roughly quadratically to cubically in the number of samples, and skip them when you need calibrated probabilities — the raw output is a signed distance, not a probability, and turning it into one requires a separate fitting step. Scale your features first, because the margin is measured in whatever units you supplied. When a straight boundary genuinely cannot work, the kernel formulation extends this same machinery.

interview.question: What does the C parameter actually control, and what do you see at each extreme?
interview.answer: C prices margin violations: it is the weight on total slack relative to the margin width. Small C buys a wide margin at the cost of misclassifying some training points, giving a smoother boundary that generalises better on noisy data. Large C forces the model to fit training points correctly, narrowing the margin and letting single outliers distort the boundary, which is overfitting in the classic sense.

interview.question: Why does an SVM depend on only a few training points, and is that an advantage?
interview.answer: The optimum's dual weights are nonzero only for points on or inside the margin, so the boundary is determined entirely by those borderline cases. It is an advantage for memory and prediction speed, since the model stores only the support vectors. It is a liability for robustness: a single mislabelled point near the boundary can become a support vector and move it, which is one reason to keep C modest on noisy data.

interview.question: When would you not use an SVM?
interview.answer: On large datasets, because training cost grows roughly between quadratic and cubic in the number of samples and becomes impractical past a few hundred thousand rows. Also when you need well-calibrated probabilities, since the decision function outputs a signed distance and Platt scaling adds a fitting step and extra variance. For large tabular problems, gradient-boosted trees usually match or beat an SVM at a fraction of the training cost.

the-kernel-trick.text: Some datasets are hopeless in their original coordinates — points of one class ringed by points of the other, with no straight boundary that works. Mapping them into a higher-dimensional space can make them separable, but writing down that mapping explicitly is often expensive and sometimes impossible, because the target space is infinite-dimensional. The kernel trick sidesteps it. Algorithms whose training only ever touches the data through inner products between pairs of points can replace each inner product with a kernel function that returns what the inner product would have been in the mapped space. You get the expressive boundary without ever computing the coordinates.
the-kernel-trick.deep_text:
Take a two-dimensional dataset where class A occupies a disc around the origin and class B forms a ring outside it. No line separates them. Now add a third coordinate equal to x squared plus y squared. The inner points get small values, the outer points get large ones, and a flat plane at a fixed height cuts them apart cleanly. Projected back to two dimensions, that plane is a circle. This is the whole idea in miniature: nonlinear in the original space, linear in the mapped space.

The trick is what makes it practical. Suppose the mapping sends a two-dimensional point to all its degree-two monomials. Computing the inner product between two mapped points means building both expanded vectors and summing the products. But that inner product happens to equal the squared inner product of the original vectors — a couple of multiplications instead of an expansion. That shortcut is the polynomial kernel. The RBF or Gaussian kernel, exp of minus gamma times the squared distance between two points, corresponds to a feature map with infinitely many dimensions, which you could never write down, yet the kernel itself is three lines of arithmetic. Mercer's condition tells you which functions are legitimate kernels: any function producing a positive semi-definite matrix of pairwise values corresponds to some inner product in some space, even if you never identify that space.

The consequence is that you never learn coordinates in the mapped space. The trained model is expressed as a weighted sum of kernel evaluations against stored training points, so prediction cost scales with how many of those points the solution retains, and the boundary's shape is set by the kernel and its hyperparameters. For RBF, gamma controls how far a single point's influence reaches: small gamma makes each point's influence broad and the boundary nearly linear, while large gamma makes influence local and the boundary wraps tightly around individual points, which is overfitting you can see by eye on a two-dimensional plot. Gamma and the regularisation strength interact, so tune them jointly on a grid rather than one at a time.

The misconception to correct is that the kernel trick is a property of support vector machines. It is not. It applies to any algorithm expressible purely in terms of inner products, which includes ridge regression as kernel ridge regression, PCA as kernel PCA, and perceptrons. SVMs are simply the most famous beneficiary because their solution is naturally written that way. A second misconception: adding dimensions does not by itself help. Randomly inflating dimensionality makes data easier to separate and easier to overfit at the same time; the kernel is useful only when its implied geometry actually matches structure in your problem, which is why RBF suits smooth local structure and a string kernel suits sequences.

Use a linear kernel first when the feature count is already large relative to sample count, as in text, since the data is usually separable already and linear training is far cheaper. Reach for RBF on low-dimensional dense data with visible curvature. Avoid kernels entirely at large n, because the kernel matrix has n-squared entries and materialising it for a million points is not an option — approximations like random Fourier features exist precisely to dodge that wall.

interview.question: Why is it called a trick rather than just a feature transformation?
interview.answer: Because the transformed features are never computed. The algorithm only ever needs inner products between pairs of points, and the kernel returns the value that inner product would take in the mapped space directly from the original vectors. For the RBF kernel the implied space is infinite-dimensional, so an explicit transformation would not even be representable, yet the kernel evaluation is trivial.

interview.question: How do you choose between a linear and an RBF kernel?
interview.answer: Start linear when the number of features is comparable to or larger than the number of samples, as in bag-of-words text, since the data is usually close to linearly separable already and linear solvers scale far better. Move to RBF when you have relatively few dense features and the linear model underfits. Validate the choice by comparing cross-validated scores, not by inspecting the data.

interview.question: What goes wrong if you set gamma too high on an RBF kernel?
interview.answer: Each training point's influence becomes extremely local, so the boundary forms tight islands around individual points. Training accuracy approaches perfect while held-out accuracy collapses — textbook overfitting. It also inflates the number of retained support vectors, which slows prediction. Gamma and the regularisation parameter must be tuned together, since a high gamma can partly mask a poor regularisation setting.

naive-bayes-and-conditional-independence.text: Naive Bayes turns classification around: instead of modelling the label given the features, it models how likely each feature value is within each class, then uses Bayes' rule to flip that into a prediction. Doing this properly would require the joint distribution over all features, which is hopeless. So it assumes something known to be false — that within a given class, every feature is independent of every other. That lets it multiply per-feature probabilities together. Training is one pass of counting, prediction is a sum of logs, and on text it stubbornly refuses to be bad.
naive-bayes-and-conditional-independence.deep_text:
Take spam filtering on 10,000 emails, 3,000 of them spam. The prior for spam is 0.3. For each word you count how often it appears in each class: suppose free appears in 900 spam emails and 100 legitimate ones, so P(free | spam) is 0.3 and P(free | ham) is roughly 0.014. An email containing free and meeting gets a score for each class equal to the prior times the product of the per-word conditionals. In practice you sum logarithms instead of multiplying, because the product of a few hundred small probabilities underflows to zero in floating point. Compare the two scores and take the larger. That is the whole model, and fitting it means incrementing counters.

One detail is not optional. If a word never appeared in spam during training, its conditional probability is zero, and a single zero annihilates the entire product regardless of the other 200 words. Laplace or add-one smoothing adds a pseudocount to every numerator and adjusts the denominator accordingly, so unseen combinations get a small probability rather than an impossible one. Skipping smoothing is the most common way to ship a broken Naive Bayes.

The independence assumption is plainly wrong. In real email, New York, and the words free and money, co-occur far more than independence predicts, so correlated evidence gets counted repeatedly and the model becomes wildly overconfident — outputs pinned at 0.9999 are routine. The important observation is that this rarely breaks the decision. Argmax only needs the correct class to score highest, not the probabilities to be right, and systematic overcounting often inflates the scores of competing classes in similar proportion. This is exactly the misconception worth naming: people discard Naive Bayes because its assumption is violated, when the assumption's violation damages its calibration far more than its ranking. Never present its probabilities as confidence to a downstream system or a user without recalibrating them.

The variants differ only in the per-feature likelihood. Multinomial Naive Bayes models word counts and is the default for text. Bernoulli models presence or absence and does better on short documents where a word appearing at all matters more than how often. Gaussian assumes each continuous feature is normally distributed within each class, storing a mean and variance per feature per class, and is the version to use on numeric tabular data — though that normality assumption is itself often shaky.

Reach for it when you want a strong baseline in minutes, when features are high-dimensional and sparse, when the training set is small and a discriminative model would overfit, or when you need online updates, since counts can be incremented as data streams in. Skip it when features are strongly correlated and you have enough data for logistic regression or a tree ensemble to learn those interactions, and skip it when calibrated probabilities matter. On the same text data, logistic regression usually edges it out given enough examples, while Naive Bayes tends to win when examples are scarce.

interview.question: The independence assumption is false for essentially every real dataset. Why does the model still work?
interview.answer: Classification only requires the correct class to receive the highest score, not accurate posterior probabilities. Correlated features cause the same evidence to be counted multiple times, which distorts the magnitudes but often distorts them in the same direction across classes, leaving the ranking intact. The damage lands on calibration: the outputs are pushed toward zero and one and should not be trusted as probabilities.

interview.question: What happens without smoothing, and why is add-one the standard fix?
interview.answer: Any feature value unseen in a class during training gets a zero conditional probability, and one zero factor drives the entire class score to zero no matter how strong the remaining evidence. Add-one smoothing gives every value a pseudocount so nothing is deemed impossible, which is equivalent to a uniform Dirichlet prior over the feature distribution. The pseudocount size is a hyperparameter worth tuning on sparse vocabularies.

interview.question: When would you pick Naive Bayes over logistic regression on a text problem?
interview.answer: When labelled data is scarce, because the generative form has higher bias and lower variance and converges to its asymptotic error with far fewer examples. Also when you need retraining to be near-instant or incremental, since fitting is pure counting and new documents can update counts in place. With plenty of labelled data, logistic regression generally reaches lower error and gives usable probabilities.
